blocks.p: "His brother," Rei said aloud. His voice came out small and flat in the air that was not air. It was the voice of a man in a kitchen. "I'm his brother. That's all I am."

blocks.cap: Rei before the man of light

blocks.p: The chair did not answer that. Behind it, the man of light did not move. Kuga's eyes held Rei's, yellow and patient. Rei felt the cat beginning to tire in his arms. There was a faint restlessness in its weight, the first warning. He did not have long. He had one question. Gin's book had been very clear about the number.

He had spent the long walk along the river deciding what to ask. How to save Gin. How to close the wall. How to kill the thing in his brother's body. Each of those was a question about power. Standing here, he had a feeling that power was the one thing this man had stopped listening to, centuries ago. So he asked the other question. The one his brother had drowned to point him toward.
"Who were you?"
The light flinched.

It was not much. A ripple ran through the cold shine of him, the way a candle flame dips when a door opens somewhere else in the house. The man did not turn. But his head moved a little toward one shoulder, the way a person half turns when he hears his name called in a crowd and is not sure it was meant for him. And the answer came into Rei the same way the lattice had shown him its history. Not in words. In pieces, out of order, like photographs dropped on a floor.

A paper lantern at dusk, hanging from a wooden roof edge, with three characters brushed on it in old ink. 逢魔時. Ōmagatoki. The twilight hour. In the old stories it is the hour between day and night when a person is most likely to meet demons. Under the characters was a small crest, as plain as an office stamp.

A notebook in a young man's hand. Its pages were full of names written very small, the way Gin wrote the things the records must never see. The hand had an ink stain on the second finger. It turned a page and kept writing. This was somebody who asked questions for a living and wrote down the answers.

A city of wooden bridges and low tiled roofs, of carts and straw sandals and swords worn at the hip. No electric wires. No neon. A river with no concrete on its banks. It was Edo, the old city that stood here for centuries before it was renamed Tokyo.

A narrow road at evening, and the young man walking along it with his shadow beside him, not behind. He did not cut the shadow off. He did not follow it either. He walked between the light and the dark the way a person walks along the top of a wall. The shadow kept pace with him like a companion he was no longer afraid of.
A plain wooden chair at the centre of everything. The young man sitting down in it, slowly, the way a person sits after a long day. The weight settling onto his shoulders. And him not getting up.

And last, smallest, a single character, like a rivet driven through all the rest. 要. It meant the pivot. The keystone. The small pin that a folding fan turns on. Rei did not know why it was there. He only knew that the man of light had held it out to him, the way a person holds out the one thing left in his pocket.

Then the pieces stopped. Behind the chair, the man's head turned back to the wall, to the work, to the thing he was holding shut. The light closed over the place where he had almost been someone. Rei felt it like a door shutting in another room. He had been answered. One question, one answer. That was the rule.
And then the chair let him reach.

That was the cruelty of it. It let his hand close the last of the distance. It let his living fingers find the edge of the empty place, where the last holder of the Thirteenth had died out of the seat and left it ringing. For one whole second he was touching the wound directly, with no glass between, the way he had wanted to touch his brother all month. In that second he read it. It was not a hole. It was an absence shaped like a hand. It was the outline of a holder who had been Duty and something more besides, two paths braided into one law. Rei's own two paths were braided the same way inside him, and he had never said so to anyone. All at once, and far too late, he understood why the Healer had wanted him here, and not only the chair. Why it had offered him the seat in his own kitchen, as mercy. The wound was shaped for a soul that walked more than one path. It had been waiting six years and longer for the right shape of hand. And the hand it had been waiting for was, near enough, his.
Then the far shore decided what he was. He was alive. And it did to him what a body does to a splinter.

There was no anger in it. That was the part he would never be able to explain afterwards, the part that would sit under his breastbone for the rest of the month. There was only the huge, patient correction of a place pushing out the one thing in it that breathed. The standing turned. The whole leaning field of attention, which had faced the centre, now faced him instead, all at once and without swinging. The not-weather went from thick to total. And the chair, the plain kitchen chair, the loudest quiet he had ever stood near, pushed. It was not a force he could brace against. It was an ending. It was the flat refusal of a closed door that has decided a man was never inside.
Kuga looked away.

The door shut at once, exactly as the page had promised. No warning. No mercy. Rei was thrown back along Gin's order in reverse, far too fast. All the half steps he had walked so carefully were used up in one backward fall. The streets got their writing back, and their depth, and their lying confidence, in flashes as he went. Canal. Konbini. Lantern. The stranger's eyes peeled off the back of his neck one layer at a time. And the last thing the far shore did, as it shut behind him, was close its hand. He felt it close around the part of him that had touched the wound. He felt the wound hold on. And he felt it tear. Not his skin. Nothing so simple. It tore the way a name tears when two people are saying it at the same time.

He came out of the water on his back. The settling pool slapped up around him in a sheet and came down on his face, warm and stinking of iron and river. Okada's hand was already under his head, keeping his mouth above the surface. Somewhere to his left a cat was complaining loudly about being wet.
"Breathe," Okada said. "Rei. Breathe first."

He breathed. The real August heat lay on him. The real security lights buzzed, and moths knocked against them. Somewhere a motorbike went over a bridge, its engine rising and fading. Beyond the pump house, the lanterns of somebody's okuribi were swinging on a real string, in a real breeze. He lay on the edge of the pool in his own moving world and looked at his hands. They had come back with him. They were no longer only his hands.
At the yard gate, the rat snake struck.

It hit the empty air above the sill so fast that Rei only saw the end of it, the long pale body snapping back into its coil. Okada was on her feet. Nothing came through the gate. The snake's head stayed fixed on the space above the graveyard earth, its tongue flicking. After a long minute it slowly lowered its chin to the concrete again.

Okada crouched beside it and laid two fingers along its back, and her eyes lost their focus. Rei had seen her do the same with a stack of files. "Small," she said at last. "Low class. It came up the trace behind you, the way water comes up a footprint. It tried the gate and the snake bit it and it went back down." She took her fingers away and looked at him. For once she did not look at his hands first. "It followed you out, Rei. Something over there has your smell now."

His hands looked like his hands, until they didn't. In the security light they were only hands, scraped at the heel from the concrete edge, shaking in the ordinary way a man shakes after a fall. Then he turned them over, and the marks were there. They were as faint as the after-image of a bright window. They lay in the lines of his palms like a second set of fingerprints under the first. He knew without being told that they were not decoration and not an injury. They were the grain of the wound, printed onto the hand that had touched it. And under the grain, finer still, was something else. It was the leftover warmth of the man at the centre, who had every path there was lit inside him, and who had answered Rei's question with a hand held out.
He flexed his fingers, and one of the lines grew warm.

For half a heartbeat, he heard a woman. Not with his ears. She was old. She was two floors up in the dark block of flats across the road, lying awake on a futon, and her thought came into him whole and tired, and it was not his. I never can sleep at Obon. He always comes and stands at the foot of the bed. Then she was gone. Rei had read people all his life, but only the space around them, the surface of the lake. Gin's book had a line for the difference. A Clairsentient knows you are angry. A Telepath knows why. That had not been the surface. That had been the water underneath.
He stood up too fast, and the world skipped.

blocks.cap: A teleport flicker that is not his

blocks.p: One moment he was on his feet at the edge of the pool. The next he was three metres along it, by the pump-house wall, with nothing in between. No step. No feeling of moving. Just here, and then there, and a hard sick lurch in his stomach, like missing a stair in the dark. Behind him on the wet concrete, his footprints ran from the edge of the pool and stopped. Then there was dry concrete. Then there was him.
Okada stared at the gap in the footprints. Kuga stopped washing himself and stared too.
"That isn't yours," Okada said quietly.
"I know."

It frightened him more than the shove had. The shove had been a door closing. This was a door left open inside his own skin. All his life he had held two paths down so hard that he had taught himself they were only one, because one was easier to carry than the truth of both. And now there was a third thing in his hands that was not even his. Abilities he had not earned and could not give back, firing on their own. And under them, a grain shaped to fit a seat that had been waiting for exactly the hand he had.

Now he understood the trap completely, the way a person understands a sentence the moment after he has said the wrong half of it. The Healer had never needed to make him take the chair. It had only needed him to touch the wound. The far shore had done the rest. It had marked him, and shaped him, and begun the long quiet work of making his hand fit the absence. The borrowed sparks would burn out. He could feel that already, the way he could feel a fever getting ready to break. But the grain under them would not. Every day he carried it, it would become a little more his and a little less borrowed. In the end he would not be able to find the difference between holding the seat and being the kind of thing that holds it.

He closed his fists over the marks, and they pulsed against his palms. Patient. Not his. Becoming his. Down the river, the real lanterns swung on their string. The real heat sat on the real water. The city breathed around him, asleep and unaware. And somewhere under all of it, leaning on a wall that rang with the shape of an empty kitchen chair, his brother was being worn by something that had just got everything it had sent him in to get.

He had come back from beyond the veil alive, which no one was supposed to do. He had come back knowing where the wound was and how it tore. He had come back with a lantern, a notebook, a road, a chair, and one small character whose meaning he could not read. And he had come back carrying the first payment of the price, printed into the only hands he had ever had to reach for Gin with. Standing by the pool with his fists shut, he did not know which he had brought home. The way to close the wall, or only the wall's way of choosing him.
